snapshot.title: UPSC Economy: National Income & Basic Concepts
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Economy Hook: GDP: Where. GNP: Who. Real: Base Year. HDI: Health/Edu/GNI. Gini: Inequality. Deflator: Nominal/Real.

quick_notes.title: GDP (Gross Domestic Product)
quick_notes.detail: Total value of all final goods and services produced WITHIN the geographical boundary of a country in a year. (Focus on "Where").
quick_notes.explanation: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total money value of all finished goods and services that are made inside a country's borders during one year. The key point is the word "Domestic," which means we only count things produced within the country's geographical boundary, no matter who owns the factory or company. For example, if a Japanese car company makes cars in India, that production is counted in India's GDP because it happens inside India. A "final good" is something sold to the end user, like a mobile phone, not the parts used to make it, so we avoid counting the same thing twice. GDP is measured in a country's currency, such as rupees for India, and it helps us see the size and health of the economy.

quick_notes.title: GNP (Gross National Product)
quick_notes.detail: Total value of final goods and services produced by the CITIZENS of a country, regardless of where they are. GNP : GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad).
quick_notes.explanation: Gross National Product (GNP) is the total market value of all finished goods and services produced in one year by the citizens of a country, no matter where in the world those citizens are working. This is different from Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which counts all production that happens within the country's physical borders, regardless of who does the producing. The difference between these two measures comes from something called Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA), which is the income earned by a country's citizens from their investments or jobs in other countries minus the income earned by foreigners inside that country. The formula is: GNP equals GDP plus NFIA. For example, the value a citizen of India creates by working in the United States is part of India's GNP but part of the United States' GDP.

quick_notes.title: Real vs Nominal GDP
quick_notes.detail: Nominal: Calculated at current market prices. Real : Calculated at base year prices (adjusts for inflation). Real GDP is the true indicator of economic growth.
quick_notes.explanation: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period. Nominal GDP is calculated using the current market prices of that year, so it can rise simply because prices have gone up due to inflation, even if no extra goods were made. Real GDP is calculated using the prices from a fixed base year, which removes the effect of inflation and shows only the change in the actual quantity of goods and services produced. Because Real GDP adjusts for rising prices, it is the true indicator of economic growth, telling you whether the economy is actually producing more, not just charging more. For example, if a country produces 10 apples at 1 rupee each, its Nominal GDP is 10 rupees; if next year it still produces 10 apples but the price rises to 2 rupees, Nominal GDP becomes 20 rupees, but Real GDP stays at 10 rupees (using the first year's price), showing no real growth.

quick_notes.title: GDP Deflator
quick_notes.detail: Ratio of Nominal GDP to Real GDP. It is a comprehensive measure of inflation in an economy.
quick_notes.explanation: The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) Deflator is a number that shows how much prices have changed in an economy over time. GDP means the total value of all goods and services produced in a country. Nominal GDP is that total value measured using today's current prices, while Real GDP is the value measured using prices from a chosen base year, so it removes the effect of price changes. The GDP Deflator is calculated by dividing Nominal GDP by Real GDP, then multiplying by 100 to get a percentage. This number tells you the overall inflation, which is the general rise in prices, across the entire economy.

quick_notes.title: HDI (Human Development Index)
quick_notes.detail: By UNDP. 3 Dimensions: 1. Health (Life expectancy). 2. Education (Mean/Expected years of schooling). 3. Standard of Living (GNI per capita).
quick_notes.explanation: HDI stands for the Human Development Index, which is a number created by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to measure how well people are doing in a country, not just by money. It looks at three main areas, called dimensions: Health, Education, and Standard of Living. For Health, it uses life expectancy at birth, which is the average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live. For Education, it looks at two things: the average number of years adults actually spent in school (mean years of schooling) and the number of years a child is expected to spend in school (expected years of schooling). For Standard of Living, it uses Gross National Income (GNI) per person, which is the total income earned by a country's people divided by the population, adjusted for the cost of living. Each dimension is given a score between 0 and 1, and the final HDI is the average of these three scores, with a higher number meaning better human development.

topic_title: UPSC Economy: National Income & Basic Concepts
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Scorecard of the Nation'. How do we measure the progress of 1.4 billion people? We explore the concepts of GDP, GNP, NNP, and the Human Development Index (HDI). For UPSC, focus on the 'Difference between Nominal and Real GDP', the 'GDP Deflator', and the various methods of calculating national income. This is the macro-foundation of the Indian Economy.
